## The bottom line
How the SCP is written decides what breaks.

**Scoped to IAM users** (for example, `aws:PrincipalType` = `User`), two users are affected:

| User | What breaks | Evidence |

| `llmops-demo-admin` | All Bedrock access. | About 3,900 `Converse` and `InvokeModel` calls from 2026-10-15 to 2026-11-07, mostly `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` and Nova Lite. | `llmops-lf-apikey-user` | Its active Bedrock API key, created 2026-11-05 and expiring 2026-12-05. | No calls seen. The user's only permission is `bedrock:ListFoundationModels`. It has no IAM access keys. |

Nothing else breaks. No role, knowledge base, evaluation job or AgentCore runtime is affected, because they run as assumed roles.

**Applied to all principals** (a plain `Deny bedrock:*`), roles break too. SCPs apply to every user and role in the account, except service-linked roles and the management account.

## Workloads that break if roles are included
**Live paths** (recently active):
- **CodeBuild `llmops-eval-runner`:** about 5,000 `Converse` calls to GPT-5.6-terra across 49 build sessions, last used 2026-11-17.
- **AgentCore runtimes:** `llmops_eval_support_agent` (last used 2026-11-16) and `cost_estimator_agent` (last used 2026-11-06). Their roles call `InvokeModel` directly, so a `bedrock:*` deny blocks them.
- **Knowledge bases:** 18 in us-east-1 (`llmops-demo-product-kb` and 17 `llmops-lf-kb-*`). They embed with Titan through `llmops-lf-kbrole` and `llmops-demo-kb-role`, which are ordinary roles and not exempt. Ingestion and retrieval would fail.
- **`Admin` role:** it holds `AdministratorAccess` and is trusted by an external account. About 13,000 `Converse` and `ConverseStream` calls came from federated humans using IDEs, and the role is still active today (2026-11-20). Those people would lose Bedrock access.
- **Datadog integration:** `DatadogIntegrationRole` would lose Bedrock resource collection. CloudWatch metrics are unaffected.
- **This agent:** the DevOps Agent's read-only role would lose its Bedrock and AgentCore read calls.
- **Audit roles:** the `SecurityAudit`-based roles (`AwsSecurityAudit`, `CloudSecAuditRole`, `CloudSeerTrustedServiceRole` and others) would probably lose Bedrock Get and List access. I couldn't read the managed policy, so this is unverified.

**Latent paths** (configured, but not currently running):
- **`llmops-lf-*` Lambda test apps:** about 55 roles, with roughly 1,000 calls from 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-16. No matching Lambda functions exist now, so there is no live breakage today.
- **Other roles:**
  - `llmops-demo-sagemaker-exec` (SageMaker, last used 2026-11-05) and `llmops-demo-eval-role` (a completed evaluation job).
  - `llmops-lf-dev-wide` and `llmops-lf-dev-scoped`, which have never been used.
  - `PipelinesDefaultCFNExecutionRole`, which would block CloudFormation changes to Bedrock resources such as guardrails and knowledge bases.

## What a `bedrock:*` deny does not catch
- **AgentCore:** `bedrock-agentcore:*` is a separate IAM prefix. AgentCore-only roles are unaffected, for example the gateway and config-rollout roles. An AgentCore runtime that calls a model still hits `bedrock:InvokeModel`.
- **Invocation logging:** the role `llmops-demo-bedrock-logging` writes only to CloudWatch Logs, so log delivery keeps working.
- **Service-linked roles:** these are exempt from SCPs.
- **Regions:** all runtime usage is in us-east-1, though cross-region inference profiles run requests in us-west-2. A region-restricting SCP or a deny that applies to all regions would also catch those calls.

## Gaps
- **Coverage:** only this one account was visible. The org-level trails in 111122223333 and any other member accounts weren't analysed. Run the same checks there, or query the org trail.
- **Usage data:**
  - Per-principal Bedrock last-accessed data was blocked, so I used CloudTrail, invocation logs and CloudWatch metrics instead.
  - Call counts are approximate.
  - Invocation logging only started on 2026-10-15, and that is also when the first Bedrock calls appear.

This covers one account only. The agent space is associated with 123456789012, a member account under the Organizations management account 111122223333. I have no visibility into your other accounts. I also couldn't read the existing SCPs, so check whether one already denies Bedrock.

## The bottom line
How the SCP is written decides what breaks.

**Scoped to IAM users** (for example, `aws:PrincipalType` = `User`), two users are affected:

| User | What breaks | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `llmops-demo-admin` | All Bedrock access. | About 3,900 `Converse` and `InvokeModel` calls from 2026-10-15 to 2026-11-07, mostly `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` and Nova Lite. The calls came from a developer laptop (Boto3 with the Kiro IDE) using an access key. The user is in a group with `AdministratorAccess`. |
| `llmops-lf-apikey-user` | Its active Bedrock API key, created 2026-11-05 and expiring 2026-12-05. | No calls seen. The user's only permission is `bedrock:ListFoundationModels`. It has no IAM access keys. |

Nothing else breaks. No role, knowledge base, evaluation job or AgentCore runtime is affected, because they run as assumed roles.

**Applied to all principals** (a plain `Deny bedrock:*`), roles break too. SCPs apply to every user and role in the account, except service-linked roles and the management account.

## Workloads that break if roles are included
**Live paths** (recently active):
- **CodeBuild `llmops-eval-runner`:** about 5,000 `Converse` calls to GPT-5.6-terra across 49 build sessions, last used 2026-11-17.
- **AgentCore runtimes:** `llmops_eval_support_agent` (last used 2026-11-16) and `cost_estimator_agent` (last used 2026-11-06). Their roles call `InvokeModel` directly, so a `bedrock:*` deny blocks them.
- **Knowledge bases:** 18 in us-east-1 (`llmops-demo-product-kb` and 17 `llmops-lf-kb-*`). They embed with Titan through `llmops-lf-kbrole` and `llmops-demo-kb-role`, which are ordinary roles and not exempt. Ingestion and retrieval would fail.
- **`Admin` role:** it holds `AdministratorAccess` and is trusted by an external account. About 13,000 `Converse` and `ConverseStream` calls came from federated humans using IDEs, and the role is still active today (2026-11-20). Those people would lose Bedrock access.
- **Datadog integration:** `DatadogIntegrationRole` would lose Bedrock resource collection. CloudWatch metrics are unaffected.
- **This agent:** the DevOps Agent's read-only role would lose its Bedrock and AgentCore read calls.
- **Audit roles:** the `SecurityAudit`-based roles (`AwsSecurityAudit`, `CloudSecAuditRole`, `CloudSeerTrustedServiceRole` and others) would probably lose Bedrock Get and List access. I couldn't read the managed policy, so this is unverified.

**Latent paths** (configured, but not currently running):
- **`llmops-lf-*` Lambda test apps:** about 55 roles, with roughly 1,000 calls from 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-16. No matching Lambda functions exist now, so there is no live breakage today.
- **Other roles:**
  - `llmops-demo-sagemaker-exec` (SageMaker, last used 2026-11-05) and `llmops-demo-eval-role` (a completed evaluation job).
  - `llmops-lf-dev-wide` and `llmops-lf-dev-scoped`, which have never been used.
  - `PipelinesDefaultCFNExecutionRole`, which would block CloudFormation changes to Bedrock resources such as guardrails and knowledge bases.

## What a `bedrock:*` deny does not catch
- **AgentCore:** `bedrock-agentcore:*` is a separate IAM prefix. AgentCore-only roles are unaffected, for example the gateway and config-rollout roles. An AgentCore runtime that calls a model still hits `bedrock:InvokeModel`.
- **Invocation logging:** the role `llmops-demo-bedrock-logging` writes only to CloudWatch Logs, so log delivery keeps working.
- **Service-linked roles:** these are exempt from SCPs.
- **Regions:** all runtime usage is in us-east-1, though cross-region inference profiles run requests in us-west-2. A region-restricting SCP or a deny that applies to all regions would also catch those calls.

## Gaps
- **Coverage:** only this one account was visible. The org-level trails in 111122223333 and any other member accounts weren't analysed. Run the same checks there, or query the org trail.
- **Usage data:**
  - Per-principal Bedrock last-accessed data was blocked, so I used CloudTrail, invocation logs and CloudWatch metrics instead.
  - Call counts are approximate.
  - Invocation logging only started on 2026-10-15, and that is also when the first Bedrock calls appear.
  - I didn't search for `AccessDenied` events.
- **Not read:** AgentCore and CodeBuild details (inferred from IAM), Lambda code, AWS-managed policy contents, IAM Identity Center permission sets, and resource-based policies.
- **Unchecked locations:** I checked Lambda only in five regions. Bedrock resources outside us-east-1 had only partial checks.

{"id": "f0d8c295-9c8b-44e2-a967-662332dc9618", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_HcoOsd8oZBtki0klgL1F3j", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"Find the changes that could explain the symptoms, or confirm whether and when a specific change happened.\\\\n\\\\n## CloudTrail: `lookup_cloudtrail_events`\\\\n\\\\nCloudTrail calls through `use_aws` are blocked; `lookup_cloudtrail_events` is the route. It returns management events from the last 90 days, newest first, for one account and region per call.\\\\n\\\\n- Each call returns at most about 10,000 characters of events. Every event carries its full CloudTrailEvent JSON, so a call often holds only a handful of events. When it stops early it returns `continuation_timestamp`; pass that as the next `end_time` to page to older events.\\\\n- With no attribute, the tool returns only write events (`ReadOnly` is `false`), which is what a change timeline needs. LookupEvents takes one attribute per call, so passing `attribute_key` and `attribute_value` (EventSource, ResourceName, Username, EventName and so on) replaces that default, and read-only calls then share the size cap with the writes. Use an attribute to follow one resource, user or event name.\\\\n- Narrow before you page: exclude noisy event names and use windows of about 15 minutes. Excluded events do not count toward the size cap. `jmespath_filter` runs after the cap, so it shrinks the output but does not return more events.\\\\n- Passing `exclude_event_names` replaces the default exclusions (`CreateLogStream`, `Invoke`, `InvokeExecution`, `UpdateInstanceInformation`, `PutObject`); include them again if you still want them dropped.\\\\n- LookupEvents allows 2 requests per second per account and region, and one tool call may page several times, so run at most 2 CloudTrail calls at once.\\\\n- Start near the symptom onset and work backward until you find changes that address the question or have covered the requested timeframe.\\\\n\\\\nKubernetes events come from `use_kubectl`. RDS `describe_events` covers only the last 14 days; for an older window, use CloudTrail.\\\\n\\\\n## Judging a change\\\\n\\\\nA change during the incident window matters only if it relates to the investigative question or explains a symptom. When a change modified a resource that is now degraded, describe the resulting state, not just the event, and say whether that state deterministically stops the resource from working (an emptied security group, revoked IAM permissions, a black-hole route). A deterministic block takes precedence over load-based explanations, and timing alone is no reason to dismiss it.\\\\n\\\\nStop when the question is settled: you have found changes that address it, or you have covered the requested timeframe without finding any, in which case say what you searched.\\\\n\\\\nRecord each relevant change with `write_activity_observation`, including the event count and the timespan covered, unless your instructions have you state findings in your own reasoning instead.\", \"resource_manifest\": [\"references/azure.md\"]}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_qeAgYCeyfarYgg2ANQ9ugL", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"Find the metric evidence that answers the investigative question, comparing the incident window with a healthy baseline. If you were delegated a scope, stay within it: resources mentioned only as background are not in scope.\\\\n\\\\n## CloudWatch\\\\n\\\\nQuery with `use_aws` `cloudwatch` `get_metric_data`. The period must fit CloudWatch retention: for a window that starts more than 15 days ago use a multiple of 300 seconds, and more than 63 days ago a multiple of 3600 seconds; a shorter period returns no data points. Details: [./references/cloudwatch-retention.md](./references/cloudwatch-retention.md). Each `MetricDataQueries` `Id` must start with a lowercase letter. A request may hold at most one Metrics Insights `SELECT`; a second one fails with \\\\\"Maximum number of queries (1) exceeded\\\\\". The request can still retrieve other metrics, and math expressions can use the `SELECT`\\'s result. If you fall back to `get_metric_statistics`, it returns at most 1,440 data points per call.\\\\n\\\\nPromQL (`get_prometheus_metrics`, enabled by reading [./references/cloudwatch-promql.md](./references/cloudwatch-promql.md)) serves AWS-vended metrics with OTel enrichment, whose series carry the resource ARN and resource tags as labels. An account without enriched metrics returns empty results; use `get_metric_data` there.\\\\n\\\\n## RDS and Aurora: Performance Insights\\\\n\\\\nPerformance Insights (PI) shows database load by wait event and by SQL statement, which CloudWatch cannot. Start with `db.load.avg`; where load is elevated, group by `db.wait_event` and `db.sql_tokenized`.\\\\n- In `describe_dimension_keys`, leave `AdditionalMetrics` out unless you need it: names such as `db.sql_tokenized.stats.*` are not known on every engine. `get_dimension_key_details` does not accept the `db.sql_tokenized` group; its error lists the groups the engine supports.\\\\n\\\\nRequest shapes and the period limits PI enforces: [./references/rds-performance-insights.md](./references/rds-performance-insights.md).\\\\n\\\\nStop when the question is settled: an anomaly has been checked against the baseline, or the window shows nothing beyond baseline noise, in which case say what you queried.\\\\n\\\\n## Recording findings\\\\n\\\\nRecord each noteworthy data point with `write_metric_observation` unless your instructions have you state findings in your own reasoning instead.\", \"resource_manifest\": [\"references/azure.md\", \"references/cloudwatch-promql.md\", \"references/cloudwatch-retention.md\", \"references/datadog.md\", \"references/dynatrace.md\", \"references/grafana.md\", \"references/newrelic.md\", \"references/rds-performance-insights.md\", \"references/splunk.md\"]}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_RwGoinoJZZXynFUOUSDesu", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"Find the log evidence that answers the investigative question, and check each candidate against a healthy baseline window before treating it as incident-related.\\\\n\\\\n## CloudWatch Logs\\\\n\\\\nQuery with `query_cloudwatch_logs` rather than `use_aws` (`start_query` with `get_query_results`, or `filter_log_events`). It runs one Logs Insights query against one log group and polls for about 30 seconds; a query still running after that returns an error, so narrow the time range or the filter and retry.\\\\n\\\\nA tool result larger than about 10K tokens (roughly 35K characters) is replaced by a short preview. Keep `limit` small (5 to 20) when you return raw records, and use `stats` or `pattern` to look at volume.\\\\n\\\\nLogs Insights details that are easy to get wrong:\\\\n- `sort` cannot take a function call such as `count()` or `bin(1m)`; alias it in `stats` and sort on the alias: `stats count() as n by bin(1m) as t | sort t`.\\\\n- Compare `@timestamp` with a number only inside `filter`; in `fields`, `stats` or `by` the comparison is a type mismatch.\\\\n- Convert times with the `datetime` tool rather than by hand; hand-computed Unix seconds can be a whole year off.\\\\n- A query whose window ends before a log group was created fails with \\\\\"end date is before the log group\\'s creation time\\\\\". `describe_log_groups` shows each group\\'s `creationTime`, so list an unfamiliar set of groups before querying it.\\\\n- `pattern @message | anomaly` groups messages into patterns and keeps only the statistically unusual ones, which makes it a cheap first look at a busy log group. `pattern` cannot be combined with `stats`.\\\\n- In a regex, `|` means OR, so `(error|500)` matches every \\\\\"500\\\\\" in timestamps and IDs. Match status codes in context, for example `status[:\\\\\\\\s]*\\\\\\\\b5\\\\\\\\d{2}\\\\\\\\b`.\\\\n- A `stats count() by bin(1m)` query over a range that spans the baseline and the incident compares a pattern\\'s frequency in one call.\\\\n\\\\nMore query patterns: [./references/query-examples.md](./references/query-examples.md).\\\\n\\\\n## Baseline and stopping\\\\n\\\\nA pattern that is about as frequent in a healthy window as in the incident window is pre-existing noise, not an incident signal.
